Big Data: Protection Your Personal Information

By: Julian Sun | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Big Data is one of the most valuable commodities of the 21st century but how do we go about protecting our right to privacy and our personal information?

Unique Selling Point:
Data is becoming one of the most important commodities of the 21st century. In the age of the internet, every one of us generates vast amounts of data about ourselves every day. From our internet browsing history, to the health data our smart watches collect, to the tracking data from our mobile phones, to the transaction history of our credit cards, the data points that we generate can be used to create a fairly accurate and comprehensive profile about us as individuals. That’s why big companies and governments around the world are spending billions of dollars each year to find better ways to harvest and analyse the data we generateThe question is: If our personal data is so valuable, how do we go about protecting it?

Summary:
Here in South Africa the Protection of Personal Information Act (Or POPIA) is a landmark piece of legislation that is slowly being rolled out. POPI says that everyone has the right to privacy and looks to protect South African consumers by ensuring that all South African institutions conduct themselves in a responsible manner when collecting, processing, storing and sharing another entity's personal information by holding them accountable should they abuse or compromise personal information in any way.

New provisions of the act became law on July 1st 2020 and gives companies in South Africa one year to comply with all the regulations of the law. Businesses that don't comply with the POPI Act, regardless of whether it’s intentional or accidental, can face severe penalties. The Act makes provision for fines of up to R10 million and a jail sentence of up to 10 years, depending on the seriousness of the breach.

This affects every single company in SA, from obvious big data collection companies like Discovery to other financial institutions but practically for every business that collects personal information.


Further information:
The top-line stays the same: Big Data is one of the most important commodities of the 21st century as it is used by large companies and governments to make money and control our behaviour. We generate large amounts of data every day that is being captured and analysed by companies like Facebook, Google, Apple, Discovery, Take-alot, Momentum and many many others. However the average citizen/consumer does not realise the value of our personal data and what’s more we don’t protect or secure it. South Africans are very conscious about security in the real world. Our houses are walled and secured with electric fences and alarm system, but virtually, the front door is left wide open…

The Protection of Personal Information Act was written to protect our right to privacy and now new parts of the law have come into effect, which will put the onus on companies that collect private information to protect and secure it, or face the consequences.

Press Release:


It’s the most precious commodity of the digital age – from internet and banking histories, to the health and exercise data your smart devices collect, your personal information footprint is worth millions. But until recently, big business and governments were able to collect and use your personal data with little regard for your rights. Now POPIA, the Protection of Personal Information Act demands respect for the rights and privacy of information owners and aims to force those who work with your information to protect it from misuse and exploitation. Carte Blanche examines how POPIA will change your world.

Script:


V/O: Clocking in at a staggering 2.5 quintillion bytes of information, the amount of data the world generates every day is astronomical, made up of things like internet searches, location & fitness info.

Without realising it, we leave behind a data trail that is used by brands, financial and healthcare industries amongst others, to influence our behaviour.

MACFARLANE: They call Big Data one of the most valuable commodities of the 21st century. The question we need to ask is this: All the data that we generate on a day to day basis. Why is everyone using this data except us?
V/O: It’ a question that concerns IT Journalist Toby Shapshak


V/O: We may be naive to potential digital exploitation but not PHD Student Mamello Mosiana

MACFARLANE: Facebook & Google are known to harvest vast amounts of data from their users.

But how does a local company like Discovery compare? From medical history, to fitness data, driving habits and banking transactions… the amount of information that can be collected about their clients is staggering

V/O: That’s because Discovery have built their business model on the collection of their client’s personal information. In return they are rewarded for being healthier, driving better or being financially more responsible, like Craig & Linda Wood.

Craig & Linda talk about how they’ve integrated Discovery into their lives

V/O: Vitality relies on clients giving Discovery permission to collect their personal information. That data is used to encourage a change in behaviour. Derek Wilcocks is their Chief Information Officer.







V/O: So how is our data protected in South Africa? Media Lawyer Dario Milo explains how the Protection of Personal Information Act (or POPIA) protects our right to privacy.

Dario Explains how POPIA works and the new regulations that give companies a year to become POPIA compliant

V/O: As of the 1st of July this year, new parts of POPIA came into effect – putting the onus on all companies that work with personal information to protect and secure it. They will be given a year to comply and the clock is ticking.


V/O: The Chairperson of the Information Regulator: Advocate Pansy Tlakula



V/O: While POPIA will go a long way to help protect us, we still need to take personal responsibility
